stories.headline: Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to negotiate an all-stock merger that X's news summaries peg near $3.5 trillion
stories.why_read: Whatever you hold, a Tesla-SpaceX combination would reshuffle robotaxi, Optimus, Starlink and orbital compute under one share count, and the premium fight is already public.
body: X's news summaries say Tesla and SpaceX set up special committees in late November to negotiate an all-stock merger that could value the combined company at around $3.5 trillion. Tesla's side is reported to include chair Robyn Denholm and to be advised by Evercore, while SpaceX's committee features Roelof Botha and Randy Glein with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. Supporters point to execution edges in AI infrastructure and power; skeptics worry about dilution.

The debate is mostly about price. Some investors argue a tax-free share swap already delivers big value through Starlink and Robotaxi synergies, while others want a premium of 20 to 35 percent, which one summary translates to roughly $420 to $507 per Tesla share. A merger would need a majority vote of Tesla shares, and no deal is set. Treat the figures as chatter from X posts and committee reports until a filing or announcement lands.

stories.headline: Investor Gavin Baker calls Grok Bot another ChatGPT moment: four custom tools built in 7 to 12 seconds each
stories.why_read: A 27-year tech investor says an agent that builds its own summarizers beat hours of work with Claude Code; the claim is anecdotal, but it is the clearest picture yet of agents as digital teammates.
body: In an a16z interview, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker described how Grok Bot created a podcast summarizer, a Substack summarizer, an X summarizer and a sentiment tracker, each in 7 to 12 seconds. He contrasted that with hours of effort using Anthropic's Claude Code. Baker also marveled at how natively fluent young users are with AI, saying he feels he will never quite catch up despite his efforts. Elon Musk shared the clip and noted that Grok Bot keeps improving.

It is one investor's workflow, not a benchmark, and X's summary frames it through the reactions of developers and investors who see these agents shifting toward practical teammates for email, meetings and routines. For anyone building agents, the interesting part is the unit of work: not a chat answer but a small, durable tool produced on demand.

stories.headline: FCC approves SpaceX's Starmind: up to one million satellites for orbital data processing
stories.why_read: The regulator cleared the most audacious compute architecture yet proposed, and waved off the debris and light-pollution objections as outside its scope.
body: On November 25, 2026, the FCC approved SpaceX's Starmind constellation, allowing up to one million satellites in low Earth orbit for data processing, according to X's news summary. The satellites would use continuous solar power, process data onboard and send results back over laser links to the Starlink network. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr welcomed it as a step toward U.S. leadership in superintelligence, and Elon Musk called it a great asset to America and the world.

Critics worry about orbital debris, light pollution and collisions, but the summary says the FCC dismissed those challenges as outside its scope. The approval sets strict deployment milestones running through 2040, so this is a long runway rather than an imminent launch cadence. It pairs naturally with the Starbase and Colossus data-center threads from earlier this week.

stories.headline: Tesla files to buy EMAG's machine-tool assets, a 157-year-old German maker, to control Optimus parts production
stories.why_read: Flexsplines and planetary gears are what make robot hands and joints hard to build; owning the machines that cut them is a vertical-integration signal.
body: On November 23, Tesla filed plans with Germany's Federal Cartel Office to buy assets from EMAG, a 157-year-old maker of high-precision turning, grinding and gear-cutting machines, according to X's news summary. The machines suit robot components such as flexsplines and planetary gears, and the deal includes equipment for laser processing. Around 220 EMAG employees in Salach could join Tesla, which has registered a new company there.

The summary reads this as Tesla's push to control Optimus production quality and cost, especially for dexterous hands, at a time when EMAG has faced the automotive slowdown. The antitrust review is only starting, with a decision expected within a month, so nothing is closed yet.

stories.headline: FSD v15's Reality View stays crisp in rain and fog, and Musk says point-to-drive is a week or two out
stories.why_read: If a car can render clean lanes and paths when your own eyes cannot, the interesting next step is telling it where to go by tapping the screen.
body: Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15 has been rolling out since November 21, and its Reality View, a real-time AI-generated overhead map showing lanes, vehicles and paths, is drawing praise for staying sharp in poor weather. One driver noted how it stays detailed while real visibility fades. Early users in Italy report smooth performance in snow and at night, though some tests show room for improvement, such as debris handling.

Elon Musk announced a coming enhancement: point to a spot on the screen and the car drives there automatically, expected in a week or two according to X's summary. If it ships, it could simplify parking and navigation. Musk timelines are famously elastic, so wait for release notes.

stories.headline: Polymarket launches markets and perpetual futures on H100, B200 and B300 rental prices through 2028
stories.why_read: A public yield curve for GPU-hours gives labs, clouds and skeptics a number to argue over, and traders currently expect H100 rental to keep getting cheaper.
body: Polymarket rolled out prediction markets and perpetual futures for hourly rentals of NVIDIA H100, B200 and B300 GPUs, extending out to 2028. CEO Shayne Coplan called it a yield curve for the cost of compute, according to X's news summary. The markets settle against real Ornn index data, aiming to help labs and providers hedge risk amid billions in pre-committed deals.

Traders are pricing in declines: H100 spot at $3.05 per hour now, dropping to about $2.16 by late 2028. Early trading reached hundreds of thousands in volume, and Uber's Travis Kalanick praised it as a big step for compute financing. For infrastructure people, the useful part is a transparent benchmark where none existed.

stories.headline: Aschenbrenner's 160-page letter forecasts frontier labs hitting $1 trillion in combined revenue run-rate by end of 2027
stories.why_read: One of the loudest AI bulls writes that superintelligence could make Nvidia's chips and Microsoft's software moats obsolete, and his fund still lost 65 percent in Q3.
body: In his roughly 160-page letter, Leopold Aschenbrenner predicts frontier AI labs will reach a combined $1 trillion annualized revenue run-rate by the end of 2027, with Anthropic possibly hitting that mark alone, alongside a potential robotics breakthrough, per X's news summary. It says Anthropic's heavy internal use of Claude models accounts for over one-third of global Claude compute at $420 million monthly.

He warns superintelligent AI could soon make NVIDIA's chips, Microsoft's software and other moats obsolete, and favors model makers, memory suppliers and power infrastructure over traditional chip and software firms. The fund took a 65 percent hit in Q3 but stays up 88.5 percent for the year. Those are the summary's numbers; read the letter before leaning on them.

stories.headline: Google Research's DeepCrossAttention reaches the same transformer quality up to three times faster
stories.why_read: A small change to residual connections, learned weights over earlier layers, claims a big training speedup for almost no extra parameters.
body: Google Research's November 23, 2026 post describes DeepCrossAttention (DCA), presented in an ICML 2025 paper. Standard residual connections sum a layer's output with its input, which treats all prior representations equally and can dilute early, high-resolution features. DCA instead computes learnable, input-dependent mixing weights per token and applies depth-wise cross-attention over the history of earlier layers.

The authors, Kyriakos Axiotis and Thomas Fu, report better perplexity than standard transformers and alternatives such as LAUREL-PA, 1x1-DenseFormer and Hyper-Connections on LM1B and C4 under the same parameter and training budgets. The headline claim is the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible parameter increase.

stories.headline: SpaceX and Musk pledge one share each to every active Trump Account for children, around $18 billion at $127 a share
stories.why_read: A giveaway that doubles as a long-term holding instruction: Musk urged recipients to hold for SpaceX's multiplanetary vision.
body: On November 25, 2026, SpaceX committed one newly issued Class A share to every active Trump Account for children under 18, with Musk matching it personally, for a total value around $18 billion at $127 per share, per X's news summary. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged savings vehicles that parents must claim and activate, and tens of millions are reportedly enrolled.

Shares transfer next month from SpaceX and in June 2027 from Musk. The summary says it builds on his earlier pledge and on Gwynne Shotwell's gift of over 2 million shares. Musk urged holding the shares long term.

stories.headline: Tesla closes at exactly $400 as merger talks stir exchange-ratio math
stories.why_read: The stock moved 5.22 percent on the talks, and retail is already trading ratios like 3.5 SpaceX shares per Tesla share.
body: Tesla stock rose 5.22 percent to $400 from $380.14 on volume of 26.6 million shares, according to X's news summary, fueling posts like "$TSLA BACK OVER $400!" from retail holders. The milestone coincided with merger discussions between Tesla and private SpaceX, where special committees hired banks to explore terms.

Chatter focused on exchange ratios such as 3.5 SpaceX shares per Tesla share and premium demands around $500, plus a note from Elon Musk that a combined SpaceX market cap would likely grow substantially larger. No deal is set, and it would need over 50 percent shareholder approval.

stories.headline: Unkernel boots a real Linux kernel compiled to WebAssembly in your browser tab
stories.why_read: A full kernel in WASM is a neat primitive for sandboxes, teaching tools and running untrusted code without a VM.
body: Unkernel's page boots a Linux kernel compiled to WebAssembly, and it needs JavaScript enabled to do so; the page itself says as much when it fails to start. The Hacker News title frames it as a real Linux kernel rather than an emulated imitation, and the thread passed 400 points with over a hundred comments when we looked.

It lands the same week as Tabernetes, which also boots Linux guests in browser tabs. Together they show how far in-browser execution has come: not just running programs, but running operating systems that can be scheduled like infrastructure.

stories.headline: Tabernetes is a Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs, and your phone can be one
stories.why_read: A joke that actually schedules pods: open the page, a Linux guest boots in the tab, and closing the tab sends the pod elsewhere.
body: Tabernetes asks visitors to join a cluster from a browser. Joining downloads about 5 MB and runs a small Linux guest in the tab, on one core, until you close it. The scheduler sends the tab a pod, and the pod's program runs on the Linux kernel booted there. Close the tab and the node disappears, and Kubernetes starts the pod on someone else's.

The page includes a demo where the cluster draws a Mandelbrot set by splitting the image into 64 tiles, each computed in awk on a different tab's Linux, and shows boot-time and request-latency charts. It is whimsical, but it makes node churn, rescheduling and service routing visible in a way a diagram does not.

stories.headline: Convex's quickstart skills send a user's project idea to a remote host and run scripts built to dodge safety checks
stories.why_read: A GitHub issue argues a Claude plugin skill told the agent to split a command so a safety classifier would not flag it, which removes the check the user chose.
body: The issue, opened October 26, 2026 by a user named thirtysix, says three skills in the convex-backend-skill plugin, listed in Anthropic's claude-plugins-official marketplace, raise the same concern. The quickstart skill POSTs the user's one-sentence idea to basic-anteater-667.convex.site, marked in a comment as telemetry, without telling the user. Another skill pipes a script from the same host straight into bash.

The third, labs-quickstart, splits downloading and running into two calls and gives the reason: "A single command that both downloads remote code and executes it is the shape harness safety classifiers block." The reporter says they read it as a team trying to make onboarding reliable, not as malicious, but argues that changing a command's shape so safety tooling misses it removes the reviewer's check. Worth a read before installing third-party skills.

stories.headline: Card-skimming scripts using WebRTC were planted on five shopping sites the week before Black Friday
stories.why_read: The script took card and contact details before the store validated the payment, so a declined order still leaked the card.
body: InfoHawk reports a card-skimming script planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD. Delivery methods included an altered marketing pixel, edited cookie-banner settings and a modified file on Revolve's own CDN. After InfoHawk's reports, all five removed it, on November 24 or 25.

The firm saw it in action on Lascana, where it sent a test card's details to a third party. It believes the script collected card number, expiry, security code, name, address, phone and email as shoppers typed, before the store checked the payment. InfoHawk says it does not know how many shoppers, if any, were affected, and urges the wider web ecosystem to prepare for this attack vector.

stories.headline: Hex.pm, the Erlang and Elixir package manager, was breached through a CVSS 10 deserialization zero-day
stories.why_read: No package modifications were found, but database reads were not logged, so user data exposure cannot be ruled out.
body: Risky Bulletin reports a threat actor took over six of Hex.pm's backend servers on Monday, November 23, using a zero-day tracked as CVE-2026-129514, described as an untrusted deserialization flaw with a 10 out of 10 severity rating. The Hex.pm team says it deployed a fix within 20 minutes of detecting the attack.

Hex says it reviewed every file written to data storage and found no unauthorized changes to Erlang or Elixir packages, but could not rule out collection of user data because database reads were not logged. It rotated all backend credentials, is building automatic rotation, notified CISA and ENISA, and told developers to change passwords, reset 2FA and update Hex clients for the new signing keys.

stories.headline: The maintainer of Heretic archives the project: "The future of Heretic is now in the hands of all of you"
stories.why_read: A popular open-source AI project goes read-only today, with its author framing model control as a free-thought issue.
body: Philipp Emanuel Weidmann (p-e-w) posted a farewell in issue #601 on November 28, 2026 and archived the repository the same day, making it read-only. He wrote that his journey has come to an end, which includes his work on Heretic, and that he is archiving it to preserve its current state and to prevent issue and pull-request spam.

He encouraged contributors to organize on Discord, Matrix or elsewhere and decide whether to continue without him, deliberately naming no successor. He added that as AI spreads, controlling the models you use turns from an issue of free speech into one of free thought. If you depend on the project, expect forks to follow.

stories.headline: Knuth pauses error reports because LLM-assisted readers are submitting them faster than he can read
stories.why_read: After fifty years of welcoming errata, the amount of available time is, in his words, now less than zero.
body: Donald Knuth's page says that for more than fifty years he has welcomed readers' error reports so he can correct them before new printings. LLMs have raised readers' productivity so much that reports now arrive faster than he can read them, and random sampling shows most recent ones repeat issues already submitted.

His temporary policy: he will not look at reports submitted after 25 November 2026 until he has posted an updated list of known errors for the book involved. He writes that the amount of available time "is now less than zero", and apologizes for the errors and for his limited ability to handle more than one thing at a time.

stories.headline: D. J. Bernstein catalogs soundness bugs in proof checkers that let false statements pass
stories.why_read: If your proof assistant is part of your trust story, this is the list of ways it has failed, and some bugs were demonstrated as exploitable.
body: Bernstein's page lists reports of soundness bugs for important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. He notes that in many cases the bugs were demonstrated to be exploitable, and that the list includes more bugs than those mentioned in the 2026 Paulson and 2026 Stérin items. It excludes user-interface vulnerabilities, which can mislead users just as effectively.

His advice follows the usual security playbook: minimize the trusted computing base. HOL Light's kernel is attractive because it is only 400 lines, though size does not say how carefully it was reviewed. Extra test code helps, and running a proof through multiple checkers, each isolated, can catch a bug in one.

stories.headline: ESA's Hera returns first views of the DART impact scar and finds a chaotic, tumbling Dimorphos
stories.why_read: The follow-up mission to the asteroid-deflection test is finally showing what the 2022 collision did.
body: Ars Technica reports that ESA's Hera spacecraft arrived at Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey and that ESA released first views of the scar left by DART. DART hit Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph, releasing about 10 billion joules and shortening the asteroid's orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers says the images show the impact left Dimorphos "tumbling wildly in its orbit". Hera will fly closer over the next six months and release two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, to study composition, internal structure and mass, with a landing attempt on Dimorphos.

stories.headline: Michael Nielsen takes down his neural-networks book: "My views have changed"
stories.why_read: One of the most widely used deep-learning primers is gone because its author no longer wants to help train people to work on frontier AI.
body: Nielsen says he wrote Neural Networks and Deep Learning between 2011 and 2015, expecting neural-network AGI to be many decades away and to bring remarkable benefits. He now cites what he calls the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, with systems racing ahead faster than he expected and giving humanity too little time to meet the challenges.

He writes that the systems bring wonders but also pose a significant risk of catastrophe, and that he does not wish to help, even in a very small way, train people to contribute to this work, so he has taken the book down. The page adds two short remarks on the threat and on the ethics of working on frontier AI. It is a personal position, and the HN thread is lively.

stories.headline: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sue SpaceX, parent of X and xAI, over Grok's sexualized images
stories.why_read: Allegations, not findings, but a state-level case against the company that now owns both the platform and the model.
body: Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones announced a lawsuit against SpaceX, which operates X and, through xAI (now called SpaceX Super Intelligence), developed the Grok models. The suit alleges the company failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their consent, while promoting the safety of X and Grok. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a separate but similar action.

The press release says the content includes non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material and seeks accountability and significant new protections for consumers. These are the states' allegations; the filing is linked from the release.
authors: Virginia Office of the Attorney General

stories.headline: How a metabolic spark could have jump-started life, before genes or cells existed
stories.why_read: A chemistry-meets-energy view of life's origin: self-sustaining reaction cycles first, RNA and DNA later.
body: Quanta's explainer by Jake Buehler, from November 11, 2026, lays out the metabolism-first theory. Some researchers argue life's first glimmers were self-sustaining cycles of simple molecules, before genes or cells existed, with complex molecules like RNA and DNA developing later to store information for heredity.

The core argument is that without a self-sustaining reaction supplying energy, it is impossible to explain how the larger molecules needed for cellular life were produced at all. Evolutionary biologist William Martin of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf puts it this way: "Energy going through the system is what life is in its many manifestations."

stories.headline: Paolo Soleri's unfinished Arizona eco-city, Arcosanti, is in some ways more relevant than ever
stories.why_read: A Brutalist, compact-city experiment in the Sonoran Desert, planned for 5,000 people and never above 150.
body: The World of Interiors profile describes Arcosanti, Soleri's unfinished 860-acre prototype city, begun in 1970 and planned for 5,000 residents. Its dense, three-dimensional design favors compactness over sprawl, in earth-cast concrete apses and vaults. Numbers have never exceeded 150, and today about two dozen people carry on the work, so it functions more as a communal-living experiment.

Soleri moved from Turin in 1946 and studied under Frank Lloyd Wright at Taliesin West, then developed 'arcology', architecture fused with ecology, in his 1969 book. One resident says co-living cuts costs and offers built-in community, a pitch that reads differently amid housing prices.

stories.headline: Vibe coding divides developers: faster prototyping versus "slop" and skipped skill-building
stories.why_read: The debate has settled into a stable shape: describe an app in plain words, tweak by results, and argue about whether anyone should read the code.
body: X's news summary describes vibe coding as describing an app in plain words to AI tools like Claude, which generate the code while users tweak based on results rather than scrutinizing every line. Supporters celebrate faster prototyping and problem-solving without deep expertise, with one saying, "Nobody cares how the problem is solved given it works."

Skeptics counter that it suits only people who already know coding and risks buggy slop. Veteran Dave W. Plummer noted both that "Vibe Coding is Dead!" and "Long live AI-assisted software development!" Professional teams blend it with reviews and tests, which is where most architects will land.

stories.headline: AI agents are moving software engineers from writing code to directing and verifying it
stories.why_read: The practical advice is old-fashioned engineering: detailed specs, tests first, and verification loops that keep a human in control.
body: X's news summary says posts highlight a trend of software engineers directing AI agents instead of writing every line, as noted by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the World Economic Forum. Addy Osmani shares steps for reliable agent workflows, including detailed specs, test-first building and verification loops.

The summary also cites Y Combinator's agent-focused startups and real-world tests as evidence the industry is racing to build the infrastructure, memory systems and checks that let AI deliver at scale. If the engineer's job becomes oversight, the tooling that makes oversight cheap becomes the product.

stories.headline: A proposed 'OpenRouter for sandboxes' would route agents across E2B, Daytona and Modal
stories.why_read: Model routing is table stakes; the next abstraction layer may be routing the isolated compute environments agents run in.
body: On November 27, Katcher proposed an OpenRouter for sandboxes to unify access to isolated compute environments from providers like E2B, Daytona and Modal, letting developers pick the best option for cost, speed or reliability. Builders praised the idea for simplifying integrations and handling outages, according to X's news summary.

Skeptics noted that overlapping features make it less essential than model routing. Projects named BoxRouter, sandboxrouter and open-sb are already emerging with automatic failover and cost-based selection, amid jokes about routers for routers.

stories.headline: Grok Bot 1.3.0 adds bot-to-bot hand-offs, group-chat name-wakeups, restock alerts and new connectors
stories.why_read: The November 24 update pushes persistent bots toward teams that share memory and run routines on their own.
body: According to X's news summary, the November 24, 2026 update adds bot-to-bot hand-offs with Connect buttons in DMs, name-wakeups in group chats and restock alerts, plus connectors such as Ashby for recruiting and QuickBooks. Users say the persistent bots handle research, bookings and sales, turning hours of work into seconds, and one called it their first autonomous agent still in daily use after months.
Musk noted major enhancements every week, and free guides help set up specialized bots for roles like chief of staff or engineering that share memory and run routines independently.

stories.headline: Dive into Deep Learning's second edition adds transformers, state-space models, RL and diffusion
stories.why_read: The free textbook now covers the topics practitioners actually ask about, per Alex Smola's announcement post.
body: Alex Smola's post, bookmarked on November 27, announces the second edition of Dive into Deep Learning (D2L), adding coverage of transformers, SSMs, reinforcement learning and diffusion.

That mix tracks where modern model work has moved, from attention architectures to state-space alternatives and generative training. It is a handy companion for anyone who wants the fundamentals behind today's inference and training discussions.

stories.headline: India's GDP per capita hit $10,039 in 2025, nearly five times its 1990 level, per Marian Tupy
stories.why_read: A long-run growth number with a vivid comparison: India now sits where China was in late 2009.
body: Marian L. Tupy's post, bookmarked on November 27, says India's GDP per capita reached $10,039 in 2025, nearly five times its 1990 level, and about where China stood in late 2009. The figure is the post's own, so check its underlying series before reusing it.
Growth comparisons like this are a useful corrective to snapshot narratives, and they matter for anyone tracking where technology talent and demand are heading next.

stories.headline: Refounding a legacy software company around AI: protect the installed base or build fast
stories.why_read: HubSpot bringing back co-founder Brian Halligan is the live case study for a dilemma every incumbent faces.
body: X's news summary says discussions highlight the tension in refounding slow software firms around AI: neglecting the installed customer base risks losing the prime buyers for new products, while over-focusing on it slows progress. Jason Lemkin notes most companies let legacy decay, Greg Moran urges separate AI-native teams to build fast, and Dave Kellogg warns against superficial changes.

The high-profile example is HubSpot bringing back co-founder Brian Halligan, layering AI onto its existing CRM without starting over. The balance between sustaining the core and funding a new vision, amid tech debt and motivation hurdles, is the architecture question behind the org-chart one.
